Your sins are forgiven you.” 9:3 Behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man blasphemes.” 9:4 Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? 9:5 For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Get up, and walk?’ 9:6 But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins-” (then he said to the paralytic), “Get up, and take up your mat, and go to your house.” 9:7 He arose and departed to his house. 9:8 But when the multitudes saw it, they marveled and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.

In this passage Jesus heals a paralytic. This event shows not only Jesus' power to heal physical illness but, more importantly, His authority to forgive sins. When the paralytic was brought to Jesus by his friends, Jesus first told him that his sins were forgiven, which stirred opposition and questioning in the hearts of the scribes present. Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked them which was easier: to say “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say “Get up and walk.” To prove that He had authority on earth to forgive sins, Jesus then commanded the paralytic to take up his mat and walk, and the man was healed. This miracle amazed all who saw it, and they glorified God.

This passage shows Jesus' supernatural power and His divine mission on earth, which is to forgive sins and heal physical sickness. By healing the paralytic, Jesus proved that He is able not only to change people's bodily afflictions but also to forgive their sins, a spiritual truth of profound depth.

Through this passage God reminds us that His power is not limited to what our eyes can see. More importantly, He cares about the condition of our hearts and our spiritual needs. Jesus' healing of the paralytic is the greatest demonstration of His love for us, and reminds us that whether our need is of body or of soul, He has the final answer and healing. We should trust Him, give our burdens to Him, and believe that He has the best plan prepared for us.
q: Reflect on your life: what spiritual or physical burdens have I not yet fully entrusted to Jesus? How can I rely on Him more, and let Him work powerfully in my life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing, through Your Son Jesus Christ, the authority to forgive and to heal. Help us, when we face physical and spiritual problems, to remember to seek Your help and guidance. Increase our faith, so that we may find comfort and strength in Your love and power. In Jesus' name we ask, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you!

v: As Jesus passed by from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax collection office. He said to him, “Follow me.” He got up and followed him.
As he sat in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and sat down with Jesus and his disciples.
When the Pharisees saw it, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.
But you go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
b: In this passage we see Jesus calling Matthew, a tax collector, to be His disciple. In those days tax collectors were regarded as sinners and traitors to society, because they collected taxes for the Roman Empire and were often accused of fraud. Yet Jesus not only called Matthew, but also ate with him and with other tax collectors and sinners. When the Pharisees questioned Jesus about eating with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus answered that He came to call sinners, not those who think they are righteous. Jesus quoted the book of Hosea: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” stressing that mercy matters more than formal religious ritual.

This passage shows how Jesus overturned the religious and social expectations of His day, challenging the self-righteousness and prejudice of the Pharisees. Jesus made clear that He came to save those who know they need saving. Jesus' actions also show how a true spiritual leader should act: welcoming everyone, especially those pushed to the margins of society.

Through this passage God reminds us that, whatever our past or present, Jesus opens His arms to us. This is good news for everyone who feels rejected or unworthy. It also challenges us to act as Jesus did: not to judge people by their appearance or past conduct, but to treat everyone with love and compassion.
q: Think about it: is there a “Pharisee-like” attitude in your life that may keep you from welcoming and loving those regarded as “unwelcome” in society? How can you show the mercy and love of Jesus more actively?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us unconditional love and acceptance through Jesus Christ. Help us to have an open heart, willing to welcome those who may be overlooked or looked down on by society. Teach us to live out true mercy and love, just as Jesus modeled on earth. In Jesus' name we ask, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you!

v: Then John’s disciples came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples don’t fast?”
Jesus said to them, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.
No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch would tear away from the garment, and a worse hole is made.
Neither do people put new wine into old wine skins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved.”
b: Matthew 9:14–17.

9:14 Then John’s disciples came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples don’t fast?” 9:15 Jesus said to them, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. 9:16 No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch would tear away from the garment, and a worse hole is made. 9:17 Neither do people put new wine into old wine skins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved.”

In this passage, John's disciples ask Jesus why they and the Pharisees often fast, while His disciples do not. Jesus answers them with the picture of a bridegroom and his guests, explaining that now is a time to celebrate, not a time to fast. He then uses the examples of mending a garment and putting wine into wineskins to illustrate the relationship between the new and the old, pointing out that something new (that is, a new age and new teaching) needs a new way to carry it.

Jesus' answer not only explains why His disciples do not fast, but also gives a deeper lesson: old religious rituals and forms cannot hold new spiritual reality. The coming of Jesus marks the beginning of a new age, and old forms (such as fasting and other traditional religious rules) may no longer fit the new teaching and the new expression of life. The pictures of new cloth and new wine show that new teaching needs a new attitude and a new approach to receive and practice it.

This passage encourages us to open our hearts to the new work and new ways of God. In the practice of our faith, we should examine whether we are clinging to tradition, or are ready to receive the renewal and change that God brings through Jesus Christ. God wants us not merely to keep outward forms but, more importantly, to be renewed in heart and obedient to His will.
q: In your life of faith, what “old wineskins” might keep you from receiving the “new wine”? How will you renew your practice, so as to better show the life and teaching of Christ?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for bringing us new life and new teaching through Jesus Christ. Help us to break free from old bonds and receive Your teaching with a fresh attitude and approach. Give us wisdom and courage to grow in Your grace and witness to Your glory. In the name of Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: While he told these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”
Jesus got up and followed him, as did his disciples.
Behold, a woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment;
for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.”
But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour.
When Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the flute players, and the crowd in noisy disorder,
he said to them, “Make room, because the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him.
But when the crowd was put out, he entered in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose.
The report of this went out into all that land.
b: Matthew 9:18–26.

9:18 While he told these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” 9:19 Jesus got up and followed him, as did his disciples. 9:20 Behold, a woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; 9:21 for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.” 9:22 But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour. 9:23 When Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the flute players, and the crowd in noisy disorder, 9:24 he said to them, “Make room, because the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him. 9:25 But when the crowd was put out, he entered in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose. 9:26 The report of this went out into all that land.

In this passage we see two important events. First, a synagogue ruler came to Jesus and begged Him to bring his daughter, who had just died, back to life. Jesus agreed to go with him. On the way, a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Jesus in faith and touched the edge of His cloak, believing that this would bring healing. Jesus praised her faith and declared that her faith had made her well, and at once she was healed. When Jesus arrived at the ruler's house, He told the mourning crowd that the girl was not dead but sleeping. Though they laughed at Him, Jesus went into the room, took the girl by the hand, and raised her to life.

This passage shows Jesus' absolute power over life and death. Whether healing a long illness or raising the dead, Jesus showed supernatural power. These two miracles show not only His compassion and power, but also stress the key role of faith in receiving God's blessing.

Through this passage God shows us that, whatever seemingly impossible situation we face, faith is the key. Faith connects us with God's power and brings about miracles. In addition, Jesus' actions teach us that even amid the doubt and ridicule of those around us, we should hold on to our conviction, and to God's promises and guidance.
q: In which areas of your life do you need to show more faith? When you face a seemingly impossible situation, how do you live out trust in God's absolute power?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us Your power and compassion through Jesus Christ. Strengthen our faith, so that in every difficulty and trial we hold firmly to Your word and Your power. When we face challenges and sickness in life, remind us to rely on You, believing that You can bring change and restoration. In Jesus' name we pray, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: As Jesus passed by from there, two blind men followed him, calling out and saying, “Have mercy on us, son of David!”
When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They told him, “Yes, Lord.”
Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you.”
Their eyes were opened. Jesus strictly commanded them, saying, “See that no one knows about this.”
But they went out and spread abroad his fame in all that land.
b: Matthew 9:27–31.

9:27 As Jesus passed by from there, two blind men followed him, calling out and saying, “Have mercy on us, son of David!” 9:28 When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They told him, “Yes, Lord.” 9:29 Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you.” 9:30 Their eyes were opened. Jesus strictly commanded them, saying, “See that no one knows about this.” 9:31 But they went out and spread abroad his fame in all that land.

In this passage we see Jesus perform the miracle of healing two blind men. The two blind men followed Jesus, crying out for mercy. When they followed Him into the house, Jesus asked whether they believed He was able to make them see. They expressed firm faith, and Jesus then worked the miracle according to their faith, and their eyes were opened. Although Jesus warned them to tell no one, in their overflowing joy they spread His fame throughout that region.

This passage highlights the importance of faith and Jesus' response to faith. Jesus not only healed their physical affliction, but also affirmed the firm faith in their hearts in His power. The actions of the two blind men, following Jesus and publicly calling Him “Son of David,” show their recognition of who Jesus is and their expectation of His power.

This passage reminds us that faith is an indispensable part of our relationship with God. When we trust fully in the power of Jesus, He will also act according to our faith. This is not only about physical healing, but about spiritual renewal and the transformation of life. Jesus welcomes those who follow Him at any cost, and responds to and blesses those who openly confess Him.
q: Looking back on your past experience, were there times when a lack of faith made you miss the chance to see God at work? How can you strengthen your trust in Jesus in hard times, so as to experience His greater works?
pr: Dear Lord, thank You for showing the power of faith in our lives. Help us to grow in trusting You, to keep seeking Your face in every circumstance. When we meet challenges and difficulties, let us remember to call upon You, and to look for Your work with firm faith. In the name of Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: As they went out, behold, a mute man who was demon possessed was brought to him.
When the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke. The multitudes marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”
But the Pharisees said, “By the prince of the demons, he casts out demons.”
Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.
Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”
b: Matthew 9:32–38.

9:32 As they went out, behold, a mute man who was demon possessed was brought to him. 9:33 When the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke. The multitudes marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!” 9:34 But the Pharisees said, “By the prince of the demons, he casts out demons.” 9:35 Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. 9:36 But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. 9:37 Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. 9:38 Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”

This passage describes Jesus working miracles and teaching the crowds. First, Jesus healed a demon-possessed man who could not speak, so that he was able to talk. This miracle amazed all who saw it, and they declared that nothing like it had ever been seen in Israel. The Pharisees, however, tried to belittle Jesus' miracle, saying that He drove out demons by the prince of demons. The passage then describes Jesus going through all the towns and villages, not only teaching people the gospel of the kingdom but also healing their sicknesses. Jesus had compassion on the crowds in their distress and helplessness, comparing them to sheep without a shepherd. Finally, Jesus called His disciples to ask God to send out more workers into the plentiful harvest.

This passage emphasizes Jesus' whole-person care for people, including the needs of body, mind and soul. By healing the mute man and by teaching, Jesus showed His power and His compassion for people. The passage also reveals the tension between Jesus and the religious leaders of the time; the Pharisees' reaction shows their hostility and misunderstanding toward Jesus.

Through this passage God reminds us that His works often go beyond what people can understand. Jesus' teaching and actions encourage us to have a larger vision, to see the needs of others and respond actively. Jesus' call for harvest workers is also a challenge to us, encouraging us to take part in God's mission and to help those who need healing in mind and body.
q: In what areas can you now become a worker in the harvest? Think about how you can more effectively engage with the spiritual and social needs of your community, and bring the gospel of the kingdom to others.
pr: Dear God, thank You for showing Your great power and boundless compassion through Your Son Jesus Christ. Stir our hearts, so that we bring spiritual light to those around us, and also bring healing and hope into their lives. Give us wisdom and courage to become Your workers, gathering souls in Your harvest. In Jesus' name we ask, amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: He called to himself his twelve disciples, and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness.
Now the names of the twelve apostles are these. The first, Simon, who is called Peter; Andrew, his brother; James the son of Zebedee; John, his brother;
Philip; Bartholomew; Thomas; Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus; Lebbaeus, who was also called Thaddaeus;
Simon the Zealot; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
Jesus sent these twelve out, and commanded them, saying, “Don’t go among the Gentiles, and don’t enter into any city of the Samaritans.
Rather, go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
As you go, preach, saying, ‘The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!’
Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, and cast out demons. Freely you received, so freely give.
Don’t take any gold, silver, or brass in your money belts.
Take no bag for your journey, neither two coats, nor sandals, nor staff: for the laborer is worthy of his food.
Into whatever city or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy; and stay there until you go on.
As you enter into the household, greet it.
If the household is worthy, let your peace come on it, but if it isn’t worthy, let your peace return to you.
Whoever doesn’t receive you, nor hear your words, as you go out of that house or that city, shake the dust off your feet.
Most certainly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city.
b: This passage describes Jesus giving the twelve disciples authority to drive out impure spirits and heal every kind of sickness. Jesus clearly instructed them to go only to the people of Israel, especially the lost sheep, and to proclaim that “the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Jesus also told them to travel simply on their mission, taking no money or extra clothing, and relying on the hospitality of the places they visited. The passage also covers how to deal with those who welcome them, and a warning for towns that refuse to receive their message.

This passage emphasizes the essence of Christian service: purity of faith and complete dependence on God. Jesus taught His disciples that serving God and spreading the gospel of the kingdom does not rely on worldly resources but on what God provides. This reminds us that in our spiritual life we should seek simplicity and purity, focusing on God's will rather than depending on material things. Jesus also reminds us that in mission work we will meet different responses; we should remain faithful, be prepared for cases where the gospel is rejected, and face them with a peaceful heart.
q: In my pursuit of the spiritual life and service, do I depend too much on material and human support? How can I learn to depend on God more deeply, and find sufficiency and contentment in all He gives? When I face rejection and challenge, how do I keep my faith and commitment to God?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the teaching and authority You have given us through Your Son Jesus Christ, so that we can serve Your kingdom in this world. Help us to learn to depend on You and not on worldly support and resources, so that our service and our lives bear witness to Your power and love. When we meet difficulty and rejection, give us strength and courage to keep walking in Your way. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: “Behold, I send you out as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you.
Yes, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the nations.
But when they deliver you up, don’t be anxious how or what you will say, for it will be given you in that hour what you will say.
For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.
“Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents, and cause them to be put to death.
You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee into the next, for most certainly I tell you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man has come.
b: This passage tells how Jesus sent His disciples out to proclaim the gospel, and told them of the persecution and trials they would face. Jesus reminded them that they would be like sheep among wolves, and must be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves, and be ready to be persecuted and to be brought before councils, governors and kings to bear witness.

This passage tells us that in the course of spreading the gospel, Christians may face all kinds of persecution and trials, but we must stand firm in faith, because the Spirit of God will speak in us and give us the words we need.

Through this passage God reminds us that faith is not smooth sailing, but His Spirit will be with us, giving us courage and wisdom to face adversity. Even when we are tested and persecuted, we must endure to the end, because the one who endures to the end will be saved.
q: When I face adversity and trials, am I willing to trust the Spirit and wisdom of God to deal with them? How can I show endurance and firm faith in adversity?
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord.
It is enough for the disciple that he be like his teacher, and the servant like his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household!
Therefore don’t be afraid of them, for there is nothing covered that will not be revealed; and hidden that will not be known.
What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in the ear, proclaim on the housetops.
Don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. Rather, fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
“Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls on the ground apart from your Father’s will,
but the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows.
b: This passage speaks of the challenges and adversity disciples may meet in proclaiming the gospel. Jesus told His disciples that a student is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master, so they should not expect to escape slander and persecution. Yet Jesus also encouraged them not to be afraid, because God knows everything and watches over each person; even the sparrows are in His sight.

The core message of this passage is to encourage disciples to stand firm in the face of difficulty and adversity, because they are watched over and protected by God. Jesus reminded the disciples to speak the truth in the open and not to shrink back in fear, because God's care matters more than anything else.

Through this passage God tells us that even when we face adversity and trials, we can rely confidently on His promises and protection. He watches over everyone; even the very hairs of our head are all numbered by Him.
q: When I face adversity and trials, am I often afraid? How can I trust God's promises and protection more firmly?
dc: Thank You, Holy Spirit, for guiding us to understand the truth and to walk in it. May God bless you.

v: Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven.
But whoever denies me before men, I will also deny him before my Father who is in heaven.
“Don’t think that I came to send peace on the earth. I didn’t come to send peace, but a sword.
For I came to set a man at odds against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
A man’s foes will be those of his own household.
He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me isn’t worthy of me.
He who doesn’t take his cross and follow after me, isn’t worthy of me.
He who seeks his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it.
b: This passage speaks of the cost of following Jesus and the impact of the gospel. Jesus declares that whoever acknowledges him before others, he will acknowledge before his Father in heaven; but whoever denies him before others, he will deny before his Father. Jesus did not come to bring earthly peace but truth and transformation, which can stir up conflict even within a family. He calls us to love him more than we love our own family, and to be willing to give up everything for him.

Through this passage God reminds us that following Jesus is not easy, yet it is an eternal value and the only way to receive true life. We should be willing to give up everything, take up the cross of Jesus and follow him, even if it means our relationships with loved ones may be affected.
q: Do we truly know that Jesus' love and grace for us surpass everything, and are we willing to let go of all things to follow him, even our love for our own family?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me.
He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward.
Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.”
b: This passage is about receiving and honoring Jesus' disciples. Jesus teaches that whoever welcomes them welcomes him, and whoever welcomes him welcomes the Father who sent him. He stresses that whether it is in the name of a prophet, a righteous person, or simply a disciple, even a cup of cold water given to someone in need will not lose its reward from God.
This passage reminds us to treat others with respect and generosity, especially those who labor for the Lord. Every small act of kindness is received and blessed by God.

Through this passage God tells us that even the smallest service, when it comes from love and goodwill, is valued and blessed by him. May we keep learning to respect and welcome others in our daily lives, and to show Christ's love through our actions.
q: How do I treat others in daily life? Am I willing to welcome and serve them with love and kindness?

v: When Jesus had finished directing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities.
Now when John heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples
and said to him, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?”
Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see:
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.
Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.”
As these went their way, Jesus began to say to the multitudes concerning John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?
But what did you go out to see? A man in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.
But why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and much more than a prophet.
For this is he, of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’
Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer; yet he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he.
From the days of John the Baptizer until now, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.
For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.
If you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah, who is to come.
b: In this passage John the Baptist sends two of his disciples to ask Jesus, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?” Jesus answers, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Blessed is he who is not offended by me.” Jesus then praises John as great, says he is the greatest of the prophets, and identifies him with the Elijah who was foretold.

This passage tells us about Jesus' mission and works, and about the role of John the Baptist. Through miracles and wonders Jesus showed that he is the Messiah, and he affirmed John's standing and calling.

Through this passage God reminds us to believe in Jesus and to find truth in his teaching and deeds. We should also follow John the Baptist's example of humility and obedience, and strive to do God's will.
q: Am I willing to follow John the Baptist's example of humility and obedience? In my life, am I able to recognize and follow the will of Jesus Christ?

v: He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call to their companions
and say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you didn’t dance. We mourned for you, and you didn’t lament.’
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is justified by her children.”
b: This passage uses a parable to describe how people of that day responded to God's truth and to his messengers. Like children calling to their playmates in the marketplace, no matter whether they played the flute or sang a dirge, the crowd could not be satisfied. John the Baptist lived a life of self-denial, yet was accused of having a demon; Jesus came living an ordinary life, yet was accused of being a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of sinners. Nevertheless, wisdom is justified by her children, who see things with wisdom and are not swayed by outside voices.

This passage shows that even when Jesus came into the world, some still refused his message because they were unwilling to change the way they lived. God reminds us to receive his word with an open heart, and to weigh things with wisdom rather than be misled by outward appearances.
q: Am I willing to see things with wisdom and not be swayed by outside influences? When I face criticism and comment, can I hold firmly to my faith and values?

v: Then he began to denounce the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they didn’t repent.
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
But I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.
You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades.  For if the mighty works had been done in Sodom which were done in you, it would have remained until today.
But I tell you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom, on the day of judgment, than for you.”
b: In this passage Jesus rebukes certain cities because they saw many of his mighty works and still did not repent. He names Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum: though they witnessed his miracles, they clung stubbornly to their sins and did not repent. Had those same mighty works been done in cities that God judged in the past, they would long ago have repented and been spared destruction.
This passage reminds us that God's grace and miracles can stir a person's heart, but repentance is our own responsibility. Without true repentance, we cannot truly receive God's grace.

Through this passage God reminds us how important repentance is. He calls us not to become proud or stubborn in sin just because we have seen his miracles, but to humble ourselves, examine our hearts, repent and turn back to God.
q: How do I respond to God's grace and miracles in my life? Am I willing to repent, accept his leading, and build a deeper relationship with him?
dc: “Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.”

v: At that time, Jesus answered, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.
Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.
All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him.
b: In this passage Jesus gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth, because he has hidden the mysteries of God from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. Jesus humbly acknowledges that this is the Father's good pleasure: God is willing to reveal truth to the humble heart.

This passage shows that God's wisdom is not measured by worldly standards. It is shown to humble and pure hearts. God's mysteries may be hidden from the wise and understanding, yet revealed to those who are willing to receive.

Through this passage God reminds us that his mysteries and wisdom are not grasped through human intelligence or learning, but are revealed to a humble and obedient heart. We should depend on God with humility, and receive his truth with the simplicity of a child.
q: Are we willing to lay down our pride and self-importance, and humbly depend on God's wisdom and guidance like little children?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for revealing your mysteries to us. May we become pure and humble disciples, willing to obey your will and let your wisdom guide our lives. Give us humble hearts that depend on your wisdom and guidance. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
b: In this passage Jesus Christ gives a gentle invitation to all who are weary and heavy laden. It is a promise of rest and renewed strength. Jesus uses the yoke as a picture. In those days a yoke was placed on the shoulders of animals so that they could pull a load together. When Jesus describes his yoke this way, it means that walking with him is an easy and light burden, because he carries our burdens with love and humility.

What God shows us through this passage is a message about dependence and trust. He encourages us to lay down the burdens of the world and turn to Jesus, seeking true rest for the soul. With Jesus we find not only rest but also how to face life's challenges with a humble and gentle heart, so that our lives become fuller and more meaningful.
q: In my daily life, where am I still carrying unnecessary burdens? How can I learn more effectively to let go of these worries and give them to Jesus, so that I can walk the road of life more lightly?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us, through your Son Jesus Christ, how to find true rest. When we face the pressures and challenges of life, help us remember to turn to Jesus and give him our worries and burdens. Teach us to be gentle and humble as Jesus is, so that our hearts may find true peace and contentment. We believe that following you brings ease and joy to life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: At that time, Jesus went on the Sabbath day through the grain fields. His disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.
But the Pharisees, when they saw it, said to him, “Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.”
But he said to them, “Haven’t you read what David did, when he was hungry, and those who were with him;
how he entered into God’s house, and ate the show bread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for those who were with him, but only for the priests?
Or have you not read in the law, that on the Sabbath day, the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath, and are guiltless?
But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here.
But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you wouldn’t have condemned the guiltless.
For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
b: In this passage Jesus answers the Pharisees' challenge about the law of the Sabbath. When his disciples, being hungry, picked heads of grain on the Sabbath, the Pharisees counted it as breaking the law. Jesus reminds them of what David did in a time of need, and of the priests who work on the Sabbath, to show that the spirit of the law matters far more than keeping its letter. He concludes that human need and mercy must rise above cold religious rules, and that he himself, the Son of Man, is Lord of the Sabbath, with authority to interpret and apply the law.

Through this passage God shows us that true faith is not blind adherence to ritual, but understanding and practicing God's love and mercy. It is a reminder that when laws and regulations become tools of oppression rather than serving people's well-being, we should re-examine their spirit and purpose. Jesus calls us to understand, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” a word that challenges us to redefine our priorities and values.
q: In my life, have I ever held on to rules so firmly that I overlooked love and mercy toward others? How can I better bring Jesus' spirit of mercy into my daily decisions and actions, especially when dealing with conflicts and challenges in my family, work or community?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the teaching of Jesus Christ, which helps us understand that you value mercy far more than outward form. Help us practice this mercy in our daily lives, so that we can treat those around us with forgiveness and understanding. When we face choices, let us remember the example of Jesus Christ and choose love and compassion over strict enforcement of the law. Give us wisdom and strength to glorify your name in everything. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: He departed from there, and went into their synagogue.
And behold there was a man with a withered hand. They asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day?” that they might accuse him.
He said to them, “What man is there among you, who has one sheep, and if this one falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, won’t he grab on to it, and lift it out?
Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.”
Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out; and it was restored whole, just like the other.
But the Pharisees went out, and conspired against him, how they might destroy him.
b: In this passage Jesus enters the synagogue and meets a man with a disabled hand. Some ask Jesus whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath; in truth they are testing him, hoping he will break the Sabbath law so that they will have grounds to accuse him. Jesus answers their test with the picture of a sheep that has fallen into a pit, to show that it is right to do good on the Sabbath. A person is worth far more than an animal, so healing and restoring health is a good deed the Sabbath allows. Jesus then heals the man's hand, showing God's power and grace, yet this stirs up even greater hostility in the Pharisees, who begin to plot how to destroy him.

Through this passage God shows us that the true purpose of law and religious ritual should be to serve people's well-being. Jesus' actions teach us to seek a balance between religious and moral rules, stressing that mercy and grace must rise above cold enforcement of law. By his actions Jesus confirms that love and mercy are at the heart of all law. This challenges us to rethink how we treat those around us, especially those who need help.
q: Think back: how did I react when someone needed my help? Do I sometimes value rules so highly that I overlook the other person's immediate need? How can I better find a balance between keeping rules and showing mercy?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for the boundless mercy and love shown through Jesus Christ. Help us to be carriers of your love and grace, not only in words but also in deeds. When we meet people in need, give us wisdom and courage to put their well-being first, rather than strict observance of rules and rituals. Let our lives be a witness to your love, showing what true Christian life looks like. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all,
and commanded them that they should not make him known:
that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying,
“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen; my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations.
He will not strive, nor shout; neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory.
In his name, the nations will hope.”
b: This passage describes how, knowing the Pharisees' hostility, Jesus chose to withdraw and continue healing. He healed all the sick among the crowds who followed him, and he warned them not to make him known. This shows his humility and his focus on the Father's will. The passage also quotes the prophet Isaiah's prophecy of the Messiah: Jesus is God's chosen servant, on whom God puts his Spirit, and who will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. Jesus acts gently and without display. He will not crush a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick, but will restore and strengthen people with compassion and justice.

Through this passage God shows us Jesus' way of serving and leading: he does not rule through power and show, but through service and grace. It reminds us that in our own life of faith we should imitate Jesus' humility and his care for the weak. His way shows that true strength lies not in loud display but in gently upholding those who need help. Such conduct brings justice into the world and hope to all peoples.
q: In which areas of my life can I serve others more humbly, especially those who feel bruised in spirit or whose hope is nearly extinguished? How can I better practice, in my community or workplace, the service and justice that Jesus modeled?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us, through the life and service of Jesus Christ, what true strength and leadership should look like. Give us Jesus' humble and caring heart, so that we may look for opportunities to help and support those in difficulty. Help us learn to reflect your love and justice in gentle and compassionate ways. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.
